introduction: “Love is greater than peace, for peace is founded upon love.” The passages gathered here, most of them from ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, treat love as the thing unity is made of: love for strangers and enemies as for friends, love for all religions and races shown in deeds, love as what holds a family, a community and at last a world together. A hundred of the guide’s three hundred quotations are given here, ten from each tenth of its length. Beside them stand a hundred voices from elsewhere: Paul’s chapter on charity, the letters of John, the Qur’an on hearts that God attunes, the Dhammapada and Spinoza on what ends hatred, Hillel, Mozi, Lincoln. About one in four does not simply agree. Machiavelli prefers fear, Kant thinks discord useful, Confucius would repay injury with justice, Burke and Mencius defend the nearer loves, and Dostoevsky’s doctor loves humanity and cannot bear his neighbour. Those end in a question.
questions: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says peace without love is only “so-called” peace; Machiavelli thinks fear the safer bond and Madison trusts a balance of rival sects. Where have you seen each kind of order, and how did it last?
“See foes as friends.” Confucius would answer injury with justice, and the Qur’an asks that hatred not make us unjust. In a real conflict you know, what would love of the enemy have meant?
Children are to be taught the love of “the humanity of humanity”. Burke and Mencius hold that love starts with one’s own. How did you learn to care about people far from you?

The condition of love, says one tablet, is that it be universal. Aristotle doubts one can be a friend to many, and Dostoevsky’s doctor loves mankind and not the man beside him. What keeps a universal love from being thin?
“Talk about things upon which we agree and say nothing about things upon which we differ.” Milton wanted truth and falsehood to grapple openly. When has each approach served unity in your experience?
Love is required towards every soul “except those who turn away”, yet enemies are to be loved. How do you read the exception beside the Sermon on the Mount?

outside.why: “Love is greater than peace, for peace is founded upon love.” Paul ranks it above faith and hope as well: the greatest of these is charity.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá says there is “a so-called peace without love”, and that it is not peace. Machiavelli advised princes that it is much safer to be feared than loved. What kind of order does each produce, and for how long?
Spiritual unity is such that “each one will make sacrifices for the other”, even of life. Jesus: greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
This unity comes “from the breaths of the Holy Spirit” and is greater than human solidarity. The Qur’an: if thou hadst spent all that is in the earth thou couldst not have attuned their hearts.
“Unity, mutual attraction, gathering together, engender life, but disunity and inharmony spell death.” Jesus: every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá reads all nature as a lesson in harmony. Kant read history otherwise: man wishes concord, but Nature knows better what is good for his species, and she will have discord. Has rivalry done any of the work that the tablet credits to unity?
Whatever led people to shun one another has been “nullified and abolished”. An Indian emperor had it cut in rock twenty-two centuries ago: whoever condemns other religions harms his own.
“See foes as friends … give to the tyrant the same great love ye show the loyal and true.” Jesus: love your enemies, do good to them which hate you.

The gazelle offers musk to the wolf. Confucius was asked about repaying injury with kindness and replied: with what then will you recompense kindness? Recompense injury with justice. Is anything owed to the difference between friend and foe?
“All the nations of the world are the sheep of God, and God is the kind shepherd.” The best-known Psalm is spoken by one of the sheep.

“Love the creatures for the sake of God and not for themselves.” Augustine divides all humanity by what it loves: self to the contempt of God, or God to the contempt of self. Is a person loved for God’s sake loved less, or more?
“Never become angry with one another.” Blake noticed what happens to anger that is never spoken: I told it not, my wrath did grow. Is the counsel never to feel anger, or never to keep it?
Love is to be shown “through deeds and not through the tongue”. John: let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth.

East and West are to “hold each other close” like two lovers. Kipling’s line that the twain shall never meet is the one remembered; his next lines say when they do. What brings them together in his ballad, and in this tablet?
Hearts must be cleansed “from even the slightest trace of hatred and spite”. Leviticus: thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart; thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá cites this saying of Jesus, about the sun and the rain, as the rule for love of all humanity. Here it is as Matthew gives it.
Whoever hates any part of humanity “violates the foundation and source of his own belief”. John: if a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar.
“Show forth the utmost love to all the peoples of the world.” The Roman playwright’s line that became a motto: nothing that concerns a man do I deem a matter of indifference to me.
The friends are to “counter sword and dagger with honey and milk”. Paul: be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.
Faithlessness met with faithfulness. The Qur’an: repel the evil deed with one which is better, and thine enemy will become as a bosom friend.
“The foundation of conflict and strife has been scattered to the winds.” Isaiah’s picture of such a world: the wolf shall dwell with the lamb.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes as though enmity were already uprooted. Yeats, in 1919: things fall apart; the centre cannot hold. Which of them was describing the world, and which a community within it?

“If religion does not become the cause of unity, its nonexistence is better than its existence.” Swift, a dean of the church: we have just enough religion to make us hate, but not enough to make us love one another.

Religion must be the cause of love. Dostoevsky’s Grand Inquisitor tells the returned Christ that the church has corrected his work and does not want him back. What happens to a religion of love when it becomes an institution?

Children are to be taught the love “not of the humanity of Asia or … Europe … but the humanity of humanity”. Burke held that to love the little platoon we belong to is the first link towards love of mankind. Can the larger love be taught first?
The humanity of humanity. Garrison printed it at the head of his paper: our country is the world, our countrymen are all mankind.
“It is my hope that spiritual fraternity shall unite the East and the West.” Schiller’s ode, which Beethoven set: all mankind are brethren.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá speaks of “the parliament of man so long dreamed of by poets”. This is the poet, and the line.
May “this strife and conflict between the peoples of the world … be eliminated”. Micah: nation shall not lift up a sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.
May each friend become “the cause of peace and harmony among all peoples, tribes and religions”. Hillel: be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace, loving mankind.
“May they establish peace with all the peoples of the world.” Paul adds two conditions: if it be possible, as much as lieth in you.
The tablet was written while “the flames of war have spread across the world”. Wilfred Owen wrote from inside those flames, of those who die as cattle.

The factions of the earth, “like bloodthirsty wolves, are tearing each other apart”. Hobbes thought both sayings true: man to man is a kind of God, and man to man is an arrant wolf. What decides which one a person meets?
One cup of the love of God can “dispel the thousand-year torpor”. Thomas à Kempis: love is a great thing; by itself it makes everything that is heavy, light.
The friends are to conquer hearts “with the sword of love”. Paul: the weapons of our warfare are not carnal.
Whoever becomes a lover of all humanity finds that “the doors of knowledge will open”. John: every one that loveth is born of God, and knoweth God.
“Do not restrict this love to the friends alone.” Jesus: if ye salute your brethren only, what do ye more than others?

Love is to reach all humanity. Aristotle observed that one cannot be a friend to many people in the full sense, any more than one can be in love with many at once. What is the love that can be given to everyone?

Love is to be such “that it becomes the cause of training both the ruler and the ruled”. Mencius and Machiavelli both wrote for rulers and gave opposite advice. What would a ruler trained by love look like?
Man is commanded to show “justice, fairness, trustworthiness … love … and kindness”. Micah’s short list: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly.

“The greatest gift is the love between hearts. However, the condition is that it must be universal.” Dostoevsky’s doctor finds that the more he loves humanity in general, the less he loves man in particular. How does a universal love stay a love of persons?
The friends are to become “a mercy to all the worlds”. The phrase is the Qur’an’s for the Prophet: a mercy for the peoples.
“We treat all nations and peoples equally.” Peter: God is no respecter of persons; in every nation he that feareth him is accepted.
All the world knows “that Bahá’ís are purely good toward all”. Tertullian records what Romans said of the Christians: see how they love one another.

Religious bigotry, when it burns in hearts, becomes “the cause of revolution, destruction, abasement”. Pascal: men never do evil so completely and cheerfully as when they do it from religious conviction.
The Founders of religion “were completely unified in love and agreement”. Rúmí: the lamps are different, but the Light is the same.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s cure for fanaticism is to see the Founders’ unity. Madison’s was institutional: many sects, so that none can oppress the rest. Which has done more, in practice, to keep the religions from each other’s throats?

Any cause “creating alienation or even ill-feeling is diabolic in origin”. Gandhi wanted not one religion but mutual respect, “unity in diversity”. Can deep disagreement go with affection, or must one give way?
Day by day “establish more rapid means of communication between the children of men”. Whitman on the canal, the railway and the cable: the lands to be welded together.
The effort is to “conciliate the hearts”. Emerson on where that begins: the only way to have a friend is to be one.

“Talk about things upon which we agree and say nothing about things upon which we differ.” Milton wanted the differences out in the open: let Truth and Falsehood grapple. When does silence about differences serve unity, and when does it only postpone the quarrel?
“Consider the members of humanity as thy own brothers and sisters.” Mozi in ancient China: regard another’s family as one’s own.
All humanity as brothers and sisters. Mencius objected that to love all equally is to acknowledge no father. What becomes of the duties one owes to actual brothers and sisters?
A united family prospers; so would a united country. Lincoln turned the Gospel sentence on his own: a house divided against itself cannot stand.
“Where unity existeth in a given family, the affairs of that family are conducted” with ease. Proverbs: better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.
“May they associate with each other in utter humility.” Paul: in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
All must be called “to friendship, to fellowship, and to divine worship”. Coleridge’s mariner: sweeter than the marriage-feast, to walk together to the kirk with a goodly company.
“Love every perfect soul even if they are not from your homeland, family or race.” Ruth, a Moabite, to her Israelite mother-in-law: thy people shall be my people.

Love is not to rest on family, nation or race, “these darknesses”. Burke defended inherited attachments: we cherish our old prejudices, and the longer they have lasted the more we cherish them. Is there anything in the love of one’s own that deserves keeping?
Believers see “the Beauty of God reflected in the soul” of one another and are drawn together. The Bible’s great friendship: the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David.
This love comes through the knowledge of God, each seeing the divine in the other. Plato’s sun is likewise what makes anything visible and lovable at all.
“When this beauteous and beloved fellowship shines in the congregation of the friends”, confirmations surround them. The Psalm: there the Lord commanded the blessing.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes to a peace society in New York. A later American, a general, counted what war costs in schools and hospitals: every gun that is made is a theft.
“If they were to set aside these acts of carnage and butchery … is it not better?” Mark Twain made a congregation hear what it was praying for when it prayed for victory.

Love is required towards every soul “except those who turn away”. Jesus allows no exception: love your enemies, pray for them which persecute you. What is the exception in the Most Holy Book protecting?
“Upon you, O loved ones of God, be unity and concord.” Paul to a divided church: that there be no divisions among you.
“Act with utmost love and unity towards all the friends and praise them all.” Paul: let all bitterness be put away; be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted.

What the tongue utters “is but a drop” of what is in the soul; unity comes “when hearts face each other”. Shakespeare thought the unspoken dangerous: give sorrow words. How much of fellowship depends on what can be said?
“Raise up the armies of love and destroy the foundation of war.” Spinoza put it as a theorem: hatred is increased by being reciprocated, and can be destroyed by love.
The tablet quotes the Light Verse for hearts that reflect one another: “light upon light”. Here is the verse.
“Though outwardly you are far from us, in reality you are in our presence.” Paul: though I be absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit.
Harmony in a gathering “createth the highest paradise”. Thoreau kept three chairs: one for solitude, two for friendship, three for society. How much company does harmony need, and how much solitude?
“Every service rendered today for the sake of God will endure.” Paul: your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
“By the absence of love, enmity increases. By the exercise of love … enmities dwindle away.” Proverbs: hatred stirreth up strifes, but love covereth all sins.
Love strengthens love. The Dhammapada states the law: hatred does not cease by hatred at any time; hatred ceases by love.
“Sow the seeds of love in the heart and not the seeds of hatred.” Paul: whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
“God cherisheth love and union, and He abhoreth enmity and oppression.” Amos has God despise even worship where justice is missing. Can there be union with an oppressor before the oppression ends?
Parents are to show sincere love to each other and educate their children accordingly. Proverbs: train up a child in the way he should go.

“There is no mightier bond in the world of being than the attachment of the heart. Even a chain of steel hath not the same degree of strength.” The Song of Solomon: love is strong as death; many waters cannot quench it.
The bond between the friends grows firmer. The Preacher: a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
The love in this meeting is “not of this world but of the world of the Kingdom”. Jesus: the kingdom of God is within you.
“With your enemies … you must show the utmost love and kindness.” Jesus on the cross: Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.
“Mutual aid and assistance is the greatest cause of success.” Kropotkin made the same phrase his answer to those who saw only competition in nature.
“Even if thy loving-kindness maketh him more bitter, manifest thou more kindliness.” The Tao Te Ching: to those who are not good to me, I am also good.

More kindness, more tenderness, however it is received. Shaw: do not do unto others as you would that they should do unto you; their tastes may not be the same. When kindness makes someone more bitter, is more of it what they need?
“If you observe any shortcomings on the part of any … be forgiving.” Peter: charity shall cover the multitude of sins.
“As soon as you see any dissatisfaction between souls, strive to create love between them.” Paul sets a deadline: let not the sun go down upon your wrath.
“Glory is not his who loveth his country, but glory is his who loveth the world.” Diogenes, asked where he came from: I am a citizen of the world.
“The purpose of human life is divine knowledge and love and kindness toward all creation.” Jesus’ summary of the law: love God, and love thy neighbour; on these two hang all.
Kindness toward all creation. Confucius, asked what benevolence is: it is to love all men.
“Ye dwell in one world, and have been created through the operation of one Will.” An American president in 1963: we all inhabit this small planet; we all breathe the same air.

Bahá’u’lláh asks hearts free of hate towards all who share one world. Adam Smith noticed that a man would lose more sleep over his little finger than over the ruin of a distant empire. What can make far-off people real to us?
Kindness wants what is best for the other and counsels them towards healing. Paul’s portrait of charity: it suffereth long, and is kind; it seeketh not her own.
The writer asked to “love the enemies”. The Qur’an holds out the hope behind such a prayer: it may be that God will ordain love between you and those with whom ye are at enmity.
Christ “was the founder of the law of non-resistance”. The law as he gave it.

Christ prayed for his enemies and taught non-resistance. The Qur’an asks something next to it: let not hatred of any people seduce you that ye deal not justly. Is justice towards an enemy less than love, or the form love takes in public life?
“I want you to open your home to all the believers and meet them all in love.” Hebrews: be not forgetful to entertain strangers.
“If we did not know Him, we should never have loved one another, for we are from different countries.” The Qur’an to the first Muslims: ye were enemies and He made friendship between your hearts.
A love “of divine origin”. Muḥammad made such love the test of faith itself.
Every human being is “a letter from the Beloved”, however blotted. Paul uses the same figure: ye are our epistle, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God.

corinthians-charity-suffereth-long.text: Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil; Rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth; Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things

corinthians-greatest-of-these.text: And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity

romans-love-fulfilling-of-the-law.text: Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law. For this, Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not kill, Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness, Thou shalt not covet; and if there be any other commandment, it is briefly comprehended in this saying, namely, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law

matthew-two-commandments.text: Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets

proverbs-love-covereth-all-sins.text: Hatred stirreth up strifes: but love covereth all sins

proverbs-dinner-of-herbs.text: Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith

peter-charity-shall-cover.text: And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins

leviticus-love-thy-neighbour.text: Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart: thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him. Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the Lord

luke-bless-them-that-curse-you.text: But I say unto you which hear, Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you, Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you

ephesians-sun-go-down.text: Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath

luke-father-forgive-them.text: Then said Jesus, Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do

matthew-kingdom-divided.text: And Jesus knew their thoughts, and said unto them, Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation; and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand

philippians-likeminded.text: Fulfil ye my joy, that ye be likeminded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind. Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves. Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others

samuel-jonathan-loved-him.text: And it came to pass, when he had made an end of speaking unto Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul

ruth-whither-thou-goest.text: And Ruth said, Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God

quran-love-and-mercy-between-you.text: And of His signs is this: He created for you helpmeets from yourselves that ye might find rest in them, and He ordained between you love and mercy. Lo! herein indeed are portents for folk who reflect.

quran-may-ordain-love.text: It may be that Allah will ordain love between you and those of them with whom ye are at enmity. Allah is Mighty, and Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.

quran-appoint-for-them-love.text: Lo! those who believe and do good works, the Beneficent will appoint for them love.

hadith-loves-for-his-brother.text: None of you will have faith till he wishes for his (Muslim) brother what he likes for himself
hadith-loves-for-his-brother.author: Muḥammad

analects-love-all-men.text: Fan Ch'ih asked about benevolence. The Master said, "It is to love all men
analects-love-all-men.author: Confucius

spinoza-hatred-destroyed-by-love.text: Hatred is increased by being reciprocated, and can on the other hand be destroyed by love
spinoza-hatred-destroyed-by-love.author: Baruch Spinoza

blake-poison-tree.text: I was angry with my Friend: / I told my wrath, my wrath did end. / I was angry with my foe: / I told it not, my wrath did grow
blake-poison-tree.author: William Blake

lincoln-better-angels.text: We are not enemies, but friends. We must not be enemies. Though passion may have strained, it must not break our bonds of affection. The mystic chords of memory, stretching from every battle-field and patriot grave to every living heart and hearthstone all over this broad land, will yet swell the chorus of the Union when again touched, as surely they will be, by the better angels of our nature
lincoln-better-angels.author: Abraham Lincoln

rights.note: Address of a President of the United States.

machiavelli-feared-than-loved.text: It may be answered that one should wish to be both, but, because it is difficult to unite them in one person, it is much safer to be feared than loved
machiavelli-feared-than-loved.author: Niccolò Machiavelli

kempis-love-is-a-great-thing.text: Love is a great thing, yea, a great and thorough good; by itself it makes everything that is heavy, light
kempis-love-is-a-great-thing.author: Thomas à Kempis
